lesson.title: Turning Scatter Into a Single Number
lesson.summary: The correlation coefficient r condenses the direction and strength of a linear relationship into one number, built directly from z-scores.
lesson.body:
Describing a scatterplot as strong is a judgment call, and two people can disagree about exactly how strong is strong. The correlation coefficient, denoted r, replaces that judgment with a single computed number that measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship, so it can be compared across data sets, reported precisely, and reasoned about without relying on anyone's eye for a graph.

The formula builds directly on z-scores, the same standardized scores used to compare individual values to a distribution. For every individual, convert its x-value into a z-score, how many standard deviations above or below the mean of x it falls, and do the same for its y-value. Multiply the two z-scores together, add up those products across all individuals, and divide by n minus 1. In symbols, r equals the sum of zx times zy, divided by n minus 1. The logic behind multiplying z-scores is simple: if an individual is above average on x whenever it is above average on y, both z-scores share the same sign, so every product is positive, and the sum builds into a large positive number. If high x tends to pair with low y instead, the signs are opposite and the products pile up negative, so a mix of matching and mismatching pairs pulls the sum toward zero rather than to either extreme.

Apply this to the five students from the previous chapter: hours studied 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and exam scores 50, 60, 65, 80, 90. The mean hours studied is 3, and the mean score is 69. The standard deviation of hours studied works out to about 1.58, and the standard deviation of scores works out to about 15.97. Converting each student to a z-score for hours and a z-score for score, then multiplying the pairs, gives products of roughly 1.51, 0.36, 0.00, 0.44, and 1.66. Adding these five products gives about 3.96, and dividing by n minus 1, which is 4, gives r equal to about 0.99.

An r of 0.99 sits extremely close to the maximum possible value of 1, confirming numerically what the scatterplot already suggested: hours studied and exam score have a strong positive linear relationship in this data set. It is worth noticing that computing r this way never required deciding which variable was more important, both were simply converted to the same standardized scale and multiplied together. Because every term in the sum is a product of two standardized scores, r carries no units of its own, one of several properties, along with a fixed range and a strange kind of symmetry, that are explored fully in the next chapter.

There is a second route to the same number that doubles as a useful check on the arithmetic above. Instead of standardizing every value first, r can also be computed as the sum of the products of the deviations from the mean, divided by the square root of the product of the sum of squared deviations in x and the sum of squared deviations in y. For this data set, the sum of the cross deviation products works out to 100, the sum of squared deviations in x works out to 10, and the sum of squared deviations in y works out to 1020, giving r equal to 100 divided by the square root of 10 times 1020, which is 100 divided by about 100.995, again about 0.99. Arriving at the same value by two genuinely different routes is exactly the kind of check worth running whenever a hand calculation matters.
